newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO, wooing Moscow, sees no need for new troops.
newsitem.headline: NATO, wooing Moscow, sees no need for new troops.

text.p: NATO has agreed not to station any permanent new troops in Europe for the foreseeable future in a move clearly aimed at meeting Russian concerns ahead of next week's presidential summit in Helsinki.
In a brief statement, issued after a meeting of NATO's 16 ambassadors on Friday, the alliance said it could currently carry out its mission of defending the West by other means.

"The Alliance will carry out its collective defense and other missions by ensuring the necessary interoperability, integration and capability for reinforcement rather than by additional permanent stationing of substantial combat forces," the statement, issued by Secretary-General Javier Solana, said.

A senior alliance diplomatic source said on Saturday the declaration was another attempt to assure Moscow the alliance's plan to expands eastwards into former communist Europe would not threaten Russia.

The latest offer by NATO forms part of a package of "sweeteners" being assembled to overcome Russia's objections to NATO's near-certain enlargement into Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic later this year and strike an accord with Moscow.

NATO has already told Moscow it has no intention of placing nuclear weapons on the territory of any members to be named at a summit in Madrid in July, has offered to make changes in arms control agreements to suit Russia, and has hinted at more financial aid.

Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov have met three times to try and sketch out a framework for a post-Cold War relationship between the two former enemies which offers Russia permanent consultations over a range of issues.
Both sides have indicated they believe major progress towards a final deal could come at the March 19-20 Helsinki summmit between Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin.
Primakov, a former Kremlin spymaster and a formidable negotiator, flies to Washington on Saturday to prepare the meeting.
He will be seeking to lay the ground for a deal with the U.S. president that could set the foundations for a new European security order.
Yeltsin, who has a good personal relationship with Clinton, said on Friday the summit would be his toughest ever but that compromise was possible.
The Russian foreign ministry has said Primakov has new proposals.

Moscow appears ready to drop demands that any NATO-Russia document should take the form of a legally-binding treaty, but is still seeking firm commitments on making sure no alliance military facilities are moved eastwards.
The alliance says Russia cannot have a veto on any NATO activities, but is willing to offer less formal commitments.
Primakov, who meets Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Saturday, Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday and Clinton on Monday, also expects serious discussion on arms control.
Russia is keen to see a reduction in sea-based nuclear missiles, an area where the U.S. has an overwhelming superiority.
